content: Choice blindness is a psychological phenomenon where individuals fail to notice significant discrepancies between their intended or expected choice and the actual outcome they receive. Psychologist Petter Johansson and his colleagues described this phenomenon in an experiment published in Science. In the experiment, participants were presented with two cards, each displaying a photograph of a different female face. They were asked to select the face they found more attractive. In the non-manipulated (NM) version of the experiment, participants were handed the card they had chosen and were asked to explain why they made that choice. In the manipulated (M) version, however, the experimenter used sleight-of-hand techniques to secretly switch the cards, giving the participant the card they had not chosen. Remarkably, most participants failed to detect the switch. Furthermore, they provided post-hoc justifications for their choice, often fabricating reasons to explain their preference. For instance, in a manipulated trial, a participant might state, I preferred this one because I like blondes, even though they had originally chosen a dark-haired woman but were handed the card with the blonde. The researchers highlighted that this experiment provides a unique opportunity to explore the relationship between decision-making and introspection. Johansson concluded that some participants, when asked to explain their choices, unequivocally generated confabulated reports—fabricated explanations that were inconsistent with their actual decisions. He suggested that studying choice blindness offers valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying truthful self-reporting.
